The documents don't define a rule keyed to two consecutive evaluation windows, so the answer depends on how the harmful-output increase is classified. If it is a safety drop of more than 2 absolute percentage points whose credible interval excludes no change, the platform should automatically roll back the canary at 97% or higher confidence [1]. If the signal is ambiguous but trending negative, it should soft-stop the canary by pausing traffic at 2x the baseline standard error and notify owners, with resumption only after manual review or completion of the automatic testing window [1]. A safety regression can also trigger rollback when it occurs alongside another medium regression, such as quality, and the composite health score falls below 0.85 of baseline [1]. For the quantized-model canaries, a failed safety-token or hallucination gate removes the canary from the routing table and sends its sessions to the configured fallback model within 30 seconds [5].

For notifications, a rollback should page on-call at high severity through PagerDuty, with the on-call playbook link in the payload, while a pause or soft-stop should send a medium-severity Slack alert [1]. Every rollback also needs a post-rollback smoke eval on the baseline prompt set, an automatically created incident ticket with the canary run summary attached, and an auto-created post-mortem [1].

Abort criteria in the documents include:
- Stage gates: hold if burn rate is between 1.0 and 2.0, and roll back automatically if burn rate exceeds 2.0 or a quality breach is detected [1].
- Immediate rollback on a sustained p99 increase above 2x baseline during a stage, or on more than 1% 5xx across the canary window [1].
- Rollback if p99 increases more than 15% within 10 minutes, or if the sustained p95 breach rate exceeds 0.5% [3].
- Automatic rollback if fence_tripped_count is above 0 and p99 uplift exceeds 10% [3]. This 10% trigger conflicts with the 15% threshold above, and the documents don't say which governs.
- Alerts at p95 increase above 5% for 3 samples, and automatic pause at a z-score above 4 on latency or throughput [4].
- Abort when 24h burn rate exceeds 3x, p99 exceeds 2x SLO for more than 5 minutes, or error rate rises more than 5x baseline over 10 minutes [5].

For rollback, freeze the canary and revert the cohort to baseline with the safe-apply revert API, and page on-call via PagerDuty with a prefilled template that includes canary_id, cohort, metric deltas and the PR link [4]. If the rollback fails, escalate to runtime-sre and divert traffic to the fallback variant [4]. After rollback, run a differential telemetry comparison, capture recent traces, and open a follow-up root-cause task. The target median time-to-rollback is under 3 minutes [3].

For dashboards, use the lane-specific p50/p90/p99 heatmap, burn-rate timeseries and error-rate histogram by tenant [1]. Also use the per-cohort latency panels, queue_length histogram and cost-delta heatmap [3], and the canary KPI dashboard with model queue depth and per-cohort p99 [4]. The per-workload SLO panel, burn-rate panel and per-tenant anomaly list are also relevant [5].

Retry-After was missing because the gateway set it only on overload rejections that its own admission control generated. When an upstream service returned a 503 overload JSON, the gateway did not normalize or add the header, so chat 503s lacked it while embeddings 429s had it [3]. Runtime saturation shed requests that only gateway sheds carried the header for [3].

The fix applies Retry-After to any response the error mapper classifies as overload, whatever its origin, unless the header is already set, and it also ensures x-redwood-request-id is present. An Control Plane guardrail limits this to stable overload codes such as `overloaded`, `breaker_open` and `dependency_overloaded`, so non-overload 5xx responses do not get it [3]. Staging verification showed Retry-After on both 429 and 503 overload responses on chat/completions and completions [3]. The ticket excerpt cuts off before any production rollout status.

For streaming, once headers are sent the gateway cannot change the status to 429, so it emits an SSE `error` event with `type=overloaded`, `code=overload_shed`, a `retry_after_ms` value of 250, and `stream_terminated=true`, followed by `[DONE]` [1]. Overload reason headers are preserved on non-streaming paths [1]. This streaming change was behind a feature flag for a us-east canary of 10% of enterprise traffic [1].

For monitoring, the plan adds a per-route metric and dashboard card for Retry-After-less 429s, with an alert when they exceed 1% above baseline for 15 minutes. It also adds a rollback trigger if 429s or errors rise more than 3% over baseline [2]. The related Retry-After and X-Redwood-Retryable header work was planned as a feature-flagged rollout [2]. The documents I was given do not confirm that the Retry-After-specific alert itself has been deployed.

**Recovery path:** Start by collecting evidence before changing anything. Request the migration runner output from the start of the step, the installer output, and the pod logs, and confirm whether any schema changes applied before the lock wait began [1]. Ask the customer DBA for a lock snapshot and any long-lived sessions from the prior attempt [1]. Do not run manual DB changes until that output is reviewed [1]. In the 2025 incident, the SRE recommendation was to scale the control plane deployments to 0 to release old connections, re-run the migration job, and restart the Postgres pod only if the job was still blocked [2]. In the February 2026 incident, the fix was for the customer DBA to terminate the one stale session holding the advisory lock, after which migrations completed [1]. If the locking session cannot be terminated safely, the guidance is to plan a rollback and reschedule the upgrade [1]. The transactional migration runner in the PR also releases the advisory lock on SIGTERM and writes a partial-state artifact [5]. For rollback, the PR describes taking a remote Terraform state snapshot before upgrading, with the installer refusing to proceed without one unless `--force` is passed [5]. Recovery then uses `bin/rwi-rollback.sh` to restore state, reapply the previous manifest set, and run `rwi-migrate --rollback <previous-sha>` [5]. Auto-downgrade of protected schema changes requires `--allow-downgrade` and a validated snapshot [5]. Manual DB downgrades should not be run [1]. The documents do not answer the customer's question about rolling back to 1.14.3.

**Artifacts to capture:** The documents point to these: installer version and target version, `kubectl describe` and logs from the migration job (for example `logs job/... --tail=200`), `kubectl get jobs` output, Postgres logs around the failure timestamp, the lock snapshot and long-lived session list, and the migration phase and last successful step [1][2]. For the PR's runner, `migrations/META.json` records the release SHA, applied time, and applied migrations [5]. The Terraform snapshot is also a required pre-upgrade artifact [5]. Customers were asked to keep logs for 7 days [1].

**Audit trail:** The documents do not define a formal audit event schema for change management. The closest records are the timestamped ticket timeline with owners and decisions [1][2], the resolution note [1], and the META.json migration record [5]. The first group didn't match because the IdP's Windows AD connector prefixed the `groups` attribute with a UTF-8 byte-order mark (bytes EF BB BF, U+FEFF). The role mapper split the comma-separated list and applied only TrimSpace, which does not remove the BOM. The first value therefore became "\uFEFFcrestline-admins", which failed the exact match against the `crestline-admins` rule, so the admin role was lost [2].

The fix was a server-side patch that runs NormalizeUnicode on attribute values before splitting, stripping the BOM and control characters [2]. The customer confirmed on 2026-03-12 that the rollout restored the admin role for the affected users, with no further 403s [2]. The documents also suggest the IdP side should strip or normalize values before export, and that a literal BOM-prefixed mapping is a less desirable workaround [2].

It was deployed to staging on 2026-03-14, where saved presets persisted after a sub-report save, and the customer confirmed the fix on the staging build [1]. The root cause is most likely a backward-compatible change in the policy-evaluation library (v2.14.0) that introduced value coercion for absent claims. When the entitlements claim is missing, the evaluator treats the subject as a single empty string, so the `not_in` membership check returns false and the exclusion rule evaluates to allow [3]. The team suspects commit 5f7e2b3 in the authorization repository, but this is still a hypothesis [3]. An earlier comment pointed to string-contains handling in `not_in` as the cause [3].

The immediate workaround was for Atlas Retail to set the entitlements claim to an empty array for service accounts and short-lived tokens. This required a small IdP mapping change [3]. The recommended interim policy change is to add an explicit `exists(user.entitlements)` check and deny when it is absent [3].

- **Prerequisites and approvals for Private deployments:** The acceptance checklist requires a contractual minimum audit retention clause, a tested on-call runbook for KMS/HSM and audit export incidents, a cutover with rollback verified in under 60 minutes, a documented quarterly access review, and a PII minimization review [1]. A post-cutover review is scheduled within 14 days [1]. Backfill is limited, and historical backfills need a separate ticket [2][3].

Security must acknowledge within 2 hours for P1/P2 [5]. Hotfixes are cherry-picked to release/hotfix/*, and feature flags are not toggled on hotfix merges [4].
3. **Build:** Prepare a single-change patch and run an offline sign-and-prove step in controlled CI [5].

For models above 1000 QPS, raise telemetry sampling for the first 30 minutes after deploy [1]. If canary shows CPU pressure but SLOs hold, use the reduced-concurrency profile for the first 24 hours [4].

The documents do not contain a single complete rollout plan, and several passages are cut off mid-sentence, so this is assembled from fragments. Several details conflict across documents, which I note where they matter.

**Staging and canary.** Start with a staging dry run that runs end-to-end integration tests under synthetic evictions [1]. Then canary at 1% of traffic across three customers with low, medium and high latency profiles, with a 72-hour monitoring window and manual approval before proceeding [1]. Another document describes a canary at 2% in us-west for 24 hours, then 20% for 72 hours before full rollout [5]. Progressive ramps are described as 0% to 1% to 5% to 25% to 100% [4]. The canary cost tolerance is also inconsistent: one passage allows at most +25% over baseline per-token cost in worst-case simulated load [1], while another allows no more than a 5% change in cost per 1,000 tokens [2].

**Metrics and thresholds.** Chat SLOs are global p95 latency of 300ms in normal operation and 600ms during fallback, for at most 5% of requests, with errors below 0.5% [1]. Canary customer-visible errors should not exceed 1.0% [2]. Quality gates vary by lane: embeddings cosine drift under 0.05 against baseline median, rerank NDCG drop under 0.03, and completions semantic similarity above 0.9 on sentinel prompts [2]. Other documents set a quality regression limit of 3% on the eval set [5], and embeddings recall drop of 6% and LM BLEU/ROUGE delta of 8% as quality-safety limits [1]. Fallback-path latency should stay under 800ms p95 for chat and completions [2]. Telemetry should track fallback_count, fallback_reason, recovery_time and fallback_success_rate [2]. Alerts should fire when fallback rate exceeds 5% over 15 minutes, quality regression exceeds 3%, or model-unavailable rate exceeds 1% [5].

**Approvals and access.** Canary progression needs manual approval [1]. The compatibility matrix needs signatures from PM, SDK and Infra [5]. A security review and any KMS routing policy update are required where fallback changes key usage [5]. Rollout actions use scoped permissions (create, update, promote, abort, view), which are enforced in Private/VPC mode [4]. Eval pass/fail can gate rollouts [3].

**Rollback and fallback rules.** Automatic fallback triggers include p95 latency above SLO for three consecutive one-minute windows, 5xx above 0.5% over five minutes, and GPU pool utilization above 92% for two minutes [1]. Rollback modes are immediate full rollback, gradual reverse rollout, and pause [3]. Abort returns to the previous stable variant [4]. Automatic rollback is specified as error rate above 2x baseline or p95 latency above 2x baseline for five minutes [2]. Customers with a pinned model get no automatic fallback and receive a 503 with a migration recommendation [5]. Cross-region fallback is opt-in and disabled by default [5].

**Customer communications.** Release notes should include migration guidance and opt-in flags for cross-region fallback [5]. Support and Solutions prepare customer comms and a migration guide [5]. A migration runbook covers opting into fallback, pinning variants, and rollback steps, and enterprise customers get migration assistance for 12 weeks after launch [5].
